Venezuela Grapples with Soaring Inflation as Currency Crisis Deepens

CARACAS, June 18 – Venezuela is facing a mounting economic crisis as the bolívar continues to lose value at a rapid pace, sparking a new wave of hyperinflation and eroding purchasing power for millions of citizens, analysts and local business leaders said Tuesday.

The bolívar fell to a record low of 14 million to the U.S. dollar on the informal market this week, marking a sharp devaluation of more than 60% in just two months. Prices for basic goods have surged in response, with the Venezuelan Confederation of Trade and Industry (Conindustria) estimating annual inflation at over 700% as of mid-June.

"We are in the midst of a financial storm," said María Teresa Rodríguez, president of Conindustria. "Businesses are struggling to keep the shelves stocked, as import costs soar and suppliers demand payment in dollars."

Residents of Caracas reported steep price hikes at markets and pharmacies, where shelves of staple items such as rice, cooking oil and medicine were often half-empty. "Yesterday I paid 80,000,000 bolívares for a kilo of chicken. Last week it was 50,000,000," said Carmen Díaz, a retired teacher shopping in the capital. "We can't keep up. Our salaries are worthless."

The Central Bank of Venezuela stopped publishing official inflation data in early May, but independent economists say the country is entering its worst hyperinflationary episode since 2018. "The government is printing money to cover deficits, and confidence in the bolívar has collapsed," said Gustavo Figueroa, an economist with the Caracas-based think tank Instituto Progreso. "We are already seeing dollarization in daily transactions, but most people simply don't have access to foreign currency."

Small businesses, from bakeries to hardware stores, have struggled to update prices fast enough to reflect the plummeting currency. "We have to change the price tags every day," said Juan Briceño, owner of the Ferretería Nacional hardware store. "Many customers are angry, but we can't sell at a loss."

Labor unions have called for urgent wage increases, warning that the minimum monthly salary, now equivalent to less than $4, is insufficient to cover even a fraction of basic needs. "Workers are being pushed into poverty," said Lourdes Castillo, spokesperson for the National Union of Public Employees.

President Luis Alberto Rivas has appealed for calm, promising new measures to stabilize the currency, but details have not been announced. Meanwhile, international aid agencies say demand for food assistance has surged, with over 8 million Venezuelans now considered food insecure.

Economists warn that unless swift action is taken to restore confidence in the bolívar, Venezuela could face further economic and social disruption in the weeks ahead.
